concepts.title: Image Registries: Docker Hub, Private Registries, and Push/Pull
concepts.description: A registry is a namespaced, content-addressable store of image manifests and layers reachable over HTTP; docker push and docker pull transfer only the layers a registry doesn't already have, and a fully-qualified image reference tells Docker exactly which registry, namespace, repository, and tag or digest to talk to -- omitting parts of that reference falls back to specific, sometimes surprising, defaults.
learningObjectives: Parse the anatomy of a fully-qualified image reference (registry host, optional port, namespace/repository, tag or digest) and state exactly what Docker assumes when parts of it are omitted.
Explain what docker push and docker pull actually transfer at the layer level, and why pushing a new tag that shares most layers with an existing image is fast.
Authenticate to a private registry with docker login and explain where those credentials are actually stored.
Explain why organizations run private registries instead of relying solely on public Docker Hub, and name at least two concrete private registry options.
Explain Docker Hub's pull rate limiting and why it disproportionately affects CI pipelines specifically.

sections.heading: Anatomy of an Image Reference
sections.body:
A fully-qualified image reference has the shape [HOST[:PORT]/]NAMESPACE/REPOSITORY[:TAG|@DIGEST], and every piece before the repository name is doing real, specific work: HOST identifies which registry to talk to at all (defaulting to Docker Hub's registry-1.docker.io if omitted entirely), an optional :PORT for registries running on a non-standard port (common for a self-hosted registry), NAMESPACE groups repositories under an organization or user account, REPOSITORY is the specific image name, and the trailing :TAG or @DIGEST pins which specific version of that repository you mean.

Docker fills in defaults very specifically when parts are omitted, and the defaults are worth memorizing exactly because they're easy to get wrong by assumption. docker pull nginx expands to docker.io/library/nginx:latest -- docker.io is the assumed host, library/ is the special namespace Docker Hub uses for its official, curated images, and latest is the assumed tag. docker pull myorg/app expands to docker.io/myorg/app:latest -- still Docker Hub, but now under the myorg namespace instead of library/. Only once you write an explicit host segment -- myregistry.example.com:5000/team/app:1.2.3, or ghcr.io/myorg/app:v2 -- does Docker route the request anywhere other than Docker Hub at all. A bare reference with no host segment always means Docker Hub, regardless of what registry you're currently logged into or have used most recently.

sections.heading: What Actually Moves Over the Wire: Layers, Not Whole Images
sections.body:
Both push and pull operate at the layer level, exactly the layers introduced in the images-and-layers module -- each identified by a content hash (digest), stored in the registry as an individually addressable blob. When you docker push an image, Docker first checks, layer by layer, whether the registry already has a blob matching that exact digest; if it does, nothing is uploaded for that layer at all, and the CLI output shows a line like Layer already exists rather than a progress bar. Only layers whose digest the registry has never seen get actually transferred.

This has a very concrete, everyday consequence: if you rebuild an image after only changing application source code, and the base image and dependency-install layers are unchanged (thanks to the cache-ordering discipline from the Dockerfile module), pushing the new build typically uploads only the one or two layers that actually changed, even though the tag now points at a 'brand new' image overall. The registry's manifest for the new tag simply lists an ordered set of layer digests, most of which it already has on file from some other tag or repository entirely -- pushing ten different tags of an application that all share the same base image effectively costs the registry (and your upload bandwidth) the price of one shared base plus ten small, changed layers, not ten full images' worth of data.

sections.heading: Authentication and Private Registries
sections.body:
docker login [registry-host] prompts for credentials (or accepts them via --password-stdin, the preferred non-interactive form that avoids leaving a password in shell history) and, on success, stores an auth token for that specific host in ~/.docker/config.json -- or, more securely, hands it off to an OS-level credential helper/keychain if one is configured, so the raw token isn't sitting in a plaintext file at all. Every subsequent docker push or docker pull against that host reuses the stored credential automatically until it's revoked or expires.

Private registries exist because Docker Hub's public model isn't the right fit for every organization's images: proprietary application code shouldn't be pushed anywhere publicly reachable at all; compliance or data-residency requirements can mandate that images never leave a specific cloud account or network; and pulling from a registry that's physically close to (or inside) the same cloud region as your deployment target is dramatically faster and more reliable than pulling over the open internet every single time. Concrete options include Docker Hub's own private repositories (same registry, access-controlled), cloud-native offerings like AWS ECR, Google Artifact Registry, and Azure Container Registry, GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io, convenient when images are built alongside code already hosted on GitHub), and self-hosted options like the open-source Docker Registry (registry:2) or Harbor for teams that want to run the infrastructure themselves. Nearly all of them implement the same underlying OCI Distribution Specification API, which is exactly why the same docker push/pull commands work against any of them with nothing more than a different host in the image reference and a docker login against that host.

sections.heading: Why Not Just Use Docker Hub for Everything
sections.body:
Beyond the private-image and data-residency reasons above, Docker Hub specifically enforces pull rate limits tied to account status: anonymous, unauthenticated pulls are capped per IP address over a rolling window, authenticated free-tier accounts get a higher cap, and paid plans remove the cap. This matters disproportionately for CI pipelines, and for a subtle, easy-to-miss reason: many CI providers run jobs from a shared pool of runners, meaning many unrelated pipelines across many unrelated organizations can end up making anonymous pulls from the exact same small set of egress IP addresses, exhausting that IP's rate limit far faster than any single team's own pull volume would suggest. A pipeline that pulled a public base image successfully all week can suddenly start failing with toomanyrequests: You have reached your pull rate limit, with nothing in that team's own usage having changed at all.

The practical mitigations are straightforward once the cause is understood: authenticate CI's pulls with a real Docker Hub account (raising the per-account limit above the anonymous-IP one), or, more robustly, mirror frequently-used public base images into a private registry or pull-through cache that the pipeline controls, decoupling build reliability from a public registry's shared, IP-based rate limiting entirely.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes: Wrong Host, Missing Tag, Missing Login
sections.body:
A push that fails with denied: requested access to the resource is denied is very often not a permissions bug at all -- it's frequently a plain mismatch between the image's local tag and the registry you're actually trying to push to. docker build -t app:1.0 . produces a local image tagged simply app:1.0, which, if pushed directly, Docker interprets as docker.io/library/app:1.0 -- Docker Hub, not whatever private registry you actually intended -- and Docker Hub correctly denies a push to a namespace you don't control. The fix is an explicit docker tag app:1.0 myregistry.example.com/team/app:1.0 (or building with that full name from the start) before pushing, so the reference actually names the intended registry and namespace.

A second common mistake is forgetting docker login before attempting a push against a registry that requires authentication at all -- producing an unauthorized error that's easy to misread as a broader access-control problem when it's really just a missing or expired login. And a third, quieter mistake is assuming that because you're logged into one registry, an unqualified image name will somehow route there -- it never does; the host segment of the reference, or its absence, is the only thing that determines which registry a command talks to, completely independent of whatever docker login sessions happen to currently be active.

examples.title: Parsing Image References and Their Defaults
examples.code:
$ docker pull nginx
# expands to: docker.io/library/nginx:latest

$ docker pull myorg/app
# expands to: docker.io/myorg/app:latest

$ docker pull ghcr.io/myorg/app:v2
# an explicit host (ghcr.io) is given -- goes to GitHub Container Registry, NOT Docker Hub

$ docker pull localhost:5000/test:dev
# an explicit host:port -- goes to a registry running locally on port 5000
examples.explanation: Each of these four references resolves to a genuinely different registry, determined entirely by whether a host segment is present and what it says. nginx and myorg/app have no host segment at all, so both default to docker.io -- the only difference between them is the namespace: library/ specifically for Docker Hub's official images versus an ordinary user/organization namespace for the second. The moment a reference includes an explicit host, like ghcr.io or localhost:5000, that host -- and only that host -- is where Docker sends the request; there's no fallback to Docker Hub, and no consultation of which registries you happen to be logged into, involved in this decision at all.

examples.title: A Rebuild That Only Pushes Changed Layers
examples.code:
$ docker build -t myregistry.example.com/team/app:1.0 .
$ docker push myregistry.example.com/team/app:1.0
The push refers to repository [myregistry.example.com/team/app]
7a3b9c1d2e4f: Pushed
f1e2d3c4b5a6: Pushed
... (base image layers) ...: Layer already exists
1.0: digest: sha256:9f8e7d6c5b4a... size: 1782

# Change only application source, rebuild, tag as 2.0, push again:
$ docker build -t myregistry.example.com/team/app:2.0 .
$ docker push myregistry.example.com/team/app:2.0
The push refers to repository [myregistry.example.com/team/app]
c9d8e7f6a5b4: Pushed          <- only the changed application-code layer actually uploads
... (base image + dependency layers) ...: Layer already exists
2.0: digest: sha256:1a2b3c4d5e6f... size: 1798
examples.explanation: The second push only actually uploads one new layer -- the one containing the changed application source -- while every layer shared with 1.0 (the base image, the installed dependencies, assuming the Dockerfile ordering from the caching module kept those separate from the source COPY) reports Layer already exists and transfers nothing at all. The registry recognizes those layers purely by their content digest, with no awareness of, or need for, any relationship between the 1.0 and 2.0 tags beyond happening to reference some of the same underlying blobs. This is exactly why pushing a new version of a large image after a small code change is typically fast -- the wire cost scales with what actually changed, not with the image's total size.

examples.title: Logging In and Fixing a Push to the Wrong Registry
examples.code:
$ docker build -t app:1.0 .
$ docker push app:1.0
denied: requested access to the resource is denied
# app:1.0 with no host segment means docker.io/library/app:1.0 -- Docker Hub, not intended at all

$ echo "$REGISTRY_TOKEN" | docker login myregistry.example.com --username ci-bot --password-stdin
$ docker tag app:1.0 myregistry.example.com/team/app:1.0
$ docker push myregistry.example.com/team/app:1.0
# succeeds
examples.explanation: The first push failed not because of a genuine permissions problem against the intended target, but because there was no intended target in the reference at all -- app:1.0 with no host segment defaults to docker.io/library/app:1.0, and pushing to Docker Hub's library/ namespace (reserved for official images) as an arbitrary user correctly gets denied. --password-stdin avoids putting a real credential into shell history or a process listing, unlike passing it as a plain --password argument. docker tag creates a second, additional name for the exact same local image, pointing at the actually-intended registry and namespace, and pushing that new reference succeeds once login against that specific host has been established.

misconceptions.description: docker push and docker pull transfer the entire image from scratch every time, regardless of what the registry or local Docker installation already has.
misconceptions.clarification: Both operate on individually content-addressed layers. Before uploading or downloading any layer, Docker checks whether that exact digest is already present on the other side, and skips the transfer entirely for any layer that already matches -- shown as Layer already exists on push or Already exists on pull. A new tag that shares most of its layers with something already stored transfers only the layers that actually differ, which is routinely a small fraction of the image's total size.

misconceptions.description: If I've logged into a private registry with docker login, an image reference with no host segment (like myapp:1.0) will push to or pull from that registry.
misconceptions.clarification: Which registry a command talks to is determined entirely by the host segment of the image reference itself -- present or absent -- never by which docker login sessions happen to be currently active. A reference with no host segment always resolves to Docker Hub (docker.io), regardless of any other registry you're logged into; reaching a different registry requires the reference to explicitly name that registry's host, typically via an explicit docker tag before pushing.

exercises.prompt: Given these three docker pull commands, which registry host does each one actually contact?
exercises.code:
$ docker pull redis
$ docker pull bitnami/redis
$ docker pull registry.example.com/internal/redis:1.0
hints: Look specifically for a host segment (something containing a dot, or a colon followed by a port, before the first slash) in each reference.
The absence of a host segment has one single, fixed default -- it's not affected by anything else you've configured.
Only the third reference contains an explicit host at all.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The first two both contact docker.io (Docker Hub) -- 'redis' expands to docker.io/library/redis:latest, and 'bitnami/redis' expands to docker.io/bitnami/redis:latest, since neither has an explicit host segment. The third explicitly names registry.example.com as the host, so it contacts that registry specifically, not Docker Hub.
exercises.solutionExplanation: docker pull redis has no slash-separated host component at all, so Docker applies its full default expansion: docker.io/library/redis:latest -- the library/ namespace is specifically reserved for Docker Hub's own official images. docker pull bitnami/redis has a namespace (bitnami) but still no host segment, so it also defaults to docker.io, just under a different namespace: docker.io/bitnami/redis:latest. Only docker pull registry.example.com/internal/redis:1.0 supplies an explicit host, registry.example.com, which is the only one of the three that contacts anything other than Docker Hub -- the presence of a dot in the first path segment is exactly the signal Docker uses to recognize it as a host rather than a namespace.

exercises.prompt: A CI pipeline runs docker build -t app:${GIT_SHA} . followed by docker push app:${GIT_SHA}, intending to push to the team's private registry at registry.internal:5000. The push fails with 'denied: requested access to the resource is denied.' Find the bug and fix it.
hints: Logging in to registry.internal:5000 doesn't change what registry the image reference app:${GIT_SHA} itself points at.
An image reference with no host segment has one fixed default, regardless of which registries you've logged into in the same script.
The build tag (or a docker tag step before push) needs to explicitly include registry.internal:5000 as the host.
exercises.solutionExplanation: app:${GIT_SHA} has no host segment, so regardless of the docker login against registry.internal:5000 that runs afterward, the push targets docker.io/library/app:${GIT_SHA} -- Docker Hub's official-images namespace -- which correctly denies an arbitrary push. Logging into a specific registry only stores a credential for use IF a command later targets that registry; it has no effect on which registry an unqualified reference resolves to. The fix is building (or re-tagging before push) with the registry host baked directly into the image reference, registry.internal:5000/team/app:${GIT_SHA}, so the reference itself, not the login state, determines the destination -- and now that destination matches the registry the login step actually authenticated against.

assessments.prompt: A developer runs docker pull myapp with no other configuration. Which registry does this actually contact, and under what namespace?
options: Whichever private registry the developer most recently ran docker login against.
docker.io (Docker Hub), under the myapp namespace directly -- there is no such thing as a namespace default for a single-word repository name.
docker.io (Docker Hub), under the library/ namespace, since a single-word repository name with no explicit namespace defaults to Docker Hub's official-images namespace.
It fails immediately, since a registry host must always be specified explicitly.
assessments.explanation: Option 3 is correct: a bare, single-word image name with no namespace or host segment expands specifically to docker.io/library/<name>:latest -- library/ being the reserved namespace Docker Hub uses for its official, curated images. Option 1 is wrong because which registries you're logged into never determines where an unqualified reference resolves to; that's governed entirely by the reference's own host segment (or lack of one). Option 2 is wrong about the specific default -- a single-word name is not treated as its own top-level namespace; it's expanded into library/. Option 4 is wrong -- omitting the host is explicitly supported and simply falls back to Docker Hub, rather than causing any kind of error.

assessments.prompt: After pushing app:1.0, a team rebuilds after only changing application source code (the base image and dependency-install layers remain unchanged), then pushes app:2.0. What does that second push actually transfer?
options: The entire image again, since each tag is stored as a fully independent copy in the registry.

Only the layer(s) whose content digest the registry has never seen before -- layers shared with app:1.0, including the base image and dependency-install layers, are skipped with a "Layer already exists" message.
Nothing at all, since the registry assumes any newly-pushed tag is identical to the immediately preceding one until proven otherwise.
Only the image's manifest, with the actual layer data synced automatically in the background sometime afterward.
assessments.explanation: Option 2 is correct: push operates layer by layer, checking each one's content digest against what the registry already has, and only genuinely new or changed layers -- typically just the one containing the changed application source, given cache-friendly Dockerfile ordering -- are actually uploaded. Option 1 is wrong -- this is exactly the misconception the concept calls out; layers are individually content-addressed and reused across tags. Option 3 is wrong -- the registry doesn't assume anything about tag similarity; it verifies each layer's digest explicitly. Option 4 is wrong -- there's no deferred background sync; the manifest and the layers it references are pushed together, with only already-present layers being skipped at push time.

assessments.prompt: A CI pipeline that has reliably pulled a public base image all week suddenly starts failing with 'toomanyrequests: You have reached your pull rate limit,' despite no change in that team's own usage. What's the most likely explanation?
options: The base image was deleted from Docker Hub, and the rate-limit message is simply a misleading error for a missing image.

Many CI providers run jobs from a shared pool of runners, so many unrelated pipelines across many unrelated organizations can end up sharing the same small set of egress IP addresses, exhausting that IP's anonymous pull rate limit far faster than any single team's own usage would suggest.
Docker Hub permanently bans any account that pulls the exact same image more than once within a 24-hour period.
The team's local Docker daemon has a corrupted image cache that needs to be manually cleared before pulls will succeed again.
assessments.explanation: Option 2 correctly identifies the subtle, easy-to-miss cause described in the concept: Docker Hub's rate limits are tied to IP address (for anonymous pulls) or account, and a shared CI runner pool means many unrelated teams' pulls can collectively exhaust one IP's limit, producing failures that have nothing to do with any single team's own pull volume. Option 1 is wrong -- a deleted image produces a distinct 'not found' error, not a rate-limit message. Option 3 is wrong -- there's no such 24-hour same-image ban; Docker Hub's actual limits are rolling-window pull counts, not per-image repetition bans. Option 4 is wrong -- a local cache issue wouldn't produce a rate-limit-specific error message from the registry itself.

assessments.prompt: What does `docker login myregistry.example.com --password-stdin` actually do, and why is --password-stdin preferred over passing the password as a plain --password argument?
options: It stores the password in a world-readable environment variable; --password-stdin only changes which variable it's stored in.

It authenticates against that host and stores an auth token (in ~/.docker/config.json or a configured credential helper), reused automatically on subsequent push/pull; --password-stdin avoids leaving the raw password visible in shell history or a process listing, unlike a plain command-line argument.
It has no meaningful security difference from --password; both approaches store the password identically in plaintext.
It only works when authenticating against Docker Hub itself, not against third-party or self-hosted registries.
assessments.explanation: Option 2 correctly describes both what login does (store a reusable auth token/credential for that specific host) and why --password-stdin is the safer form (a plain --password argument can be captured in shell history or observed via a process listing, while stdin avoids both). Option 1 invents an environment-variable storage mechanism that isn't how docker login actually stores credentials. Option 3 is wrong -- the whole point of the concept's guidance is that --password-stdin meaningfully reduces exposure compared to a plain argument. Option 4 is wrong -- docker login works identically against any registry implementing the standard registry API, including self-hosted and third-party ones, not just Docker Hub.

assessments.prompt: Explain, at the level of layers and content digests, why pushing a new tag of an image that shares most of its layers with an image already in the registry is typically fast, and separately, explain why an organization might choose to run a private registry instead of relying entirely on public Docker Hub.
assessments.modelAnswer: A registry stores image layers as individually content-addressed blobs, each identified by a digest computed from that layer's own actual content -- it has no inherent concept of one image being 'a newer version of' another beyond whatever digests their respective manifests happen to list. When docker push runs, Docker checks, layer by layer, whether the registry already holds a blob matching that exact digest; any layer that matches is skipped entirely, with only genuinely new or changed layers actually transferred over the wire. Because a typical rebuild -- especially one following the cache-friendly Dockerfile ordering from the earlier module -- usually only changes the layer or two containing application source, while the base image and dependency-installation layers stay byte-for-byte identical, pushing a new tag after a small code change tends to upload only that small changed portion, even though the tag conceptually represents 'a whole new image.' The registry's manifest for the new tag is really just a new, small pointer document listing an ordered set of layer digests -- most of which the registry already has on file, whether from an earlier tag of the same repository or an entirely unrelated one that happened to share a base image. As for private registries: organizations run them for reasons beyond simple preference. Proprietary application code generally shouldn't be pushed anywhere publicly reachable, which rules out plain public Docker Hub repositories for most real production images; some organizations operate under compliance or data-residency requirements that mandate images never leave a specific network, cloud account, or geographic region, which a self-hosted or cloud-provider-specific private registry can satisfy in a way a shared public registry cannot; and a registry located physically close to, or inside, the same network as the systems actually pulling from it -- a cloud-native registry in the same region as a Kubernetes cluster, for instance -- pulls dramatically faster and more reliably than repeatedly fetching the same layers over the open internet, which matters directly for deploy speed and for the reliability of automated pipelines that pull images frequently.

concepts.title: Tagging Strategies: Why :latest Is Dangerous in Production
concepts.description: A tag is nothing more than a mutable, human-readable pointer to whichever manifest digest was most recently pushed under that name -- :latest is simply the tag Docker applies by default when none is given, with no enforced meaning of recency, stability, or correctness, which is exactly why relying on it in production quietly removes your ability to roll back, trace, or reproduce what's actually running.
learningObjectives: Explain precisely what a tag is (a mutable pointer to a single manifest digest at any given moment) and how that differs fundamentally from a digest.
Explain why :latest has never meant, and was never designed to guarantee, 'the most recently built or most stable image' -- only 'the tag applied by default when none is specified.'

Identify at least three concrete production problems caused by deploying against :latest: no rollback target, replica drift during a rolling deploy, and no audit trail back to the code that produced a running container.
Design a practical multi-tag scheme for a CI/CD pipeline combining an immutable identifier, a semantic version, and an optional floating convenience tag, and explain what each is for.
Explain what pinning a deployment to an image digest buys over even an apparently-immutable version tag, and when that extra rigor is worth its cost.

sections.heading: A Tag Is a Pointer, Not a Version
sections.body:
A registry maps each (repository, tag) pair to exactly one manifest digest at any given moment -- and nothing more permanent than that. Pushing to an existing tag name simply reassigns that mapping to point at a new digest; the old digest may still physically exist in the registry for a while (until garbage collection or explicit deletion), but the tag itself now points somewhere else, instantly, for every future pull. There is no versioning, history, or append-only guarantee built into a tag by default -- it behaves much more like a mutable variable than like a git tag or a release number, despite superficially looking similar in a docker images listing.

:latest is exactly this mechanism, applied to one specific, unremarkable string: it's simply the tag Docker assigns automatically to a build or push that doesn't specify a tag at all. Nothing about the name enforces recency ('the actual most recent build') or quality ('the most stable, tested build') -- it's whatever was most recently pushed under that literal tag name, by whoever had push access, which could be an experimental branch build, a broken hotfix that got reverted five minutes later, or a genuinely solid release, with the tag itself carrying no information distinguishing between those cases.

sections.heading: The Concrete Failure Modes of :latest in Production
sections.body:
Three specific, recurring problems follow directly from treating a mutable pointer as a deployment target. First, there is no rollback target: if whatever :latest currently points at turns out to be broken, 'roll back to the previous latest' isn't actually a coherent operation, because the previous digest that tag used to point at has already been overwritten in the mapping -- recovering it requires either the registry still physically retaining that old, now-untagged digest and someone knowing what it was, or rebuilding from source and hoping the rebuild is reproducible enough to match, which the reproducibility module already established is not a safe assumption unless the Dockerfile and its dependencies were rigorously pinned.

Second, replica drift: during a rolling deploy of several replicas, each one typically pulls the image independently, at a slightly different moment. If a new push to :latest lands in the middle of that rollout window, some replicas can end up running the previous content and others the new content simultaneously, purely due to timing -- a real, observable form of inconsistency that has nothing to do with any bug in the application itself, and everything to do with the tag's mapping changing out from under an in-progress rollout.

Third, and perhaps most damaging during an actual incident: untraceability. Given a running container built from :latest, there is no way to look at that tag alone and determine which git commit, which dependency versions, or which build produced it -- the tag simply doesn't carry that information, and by the time you're debugging a production incident, the very same tag may already be pointing at something different again if anyone has pushed since. Incident response routinely needs exactly this kind of provenance, and :latest structurally cannot provide it.

sections.heading: A Practical Multi-Tag Scheme
sections.body:
Real CI/CD pipelines typically push several tags for the exact same build simultaneously, each serving a distinct purpose:

```bash
docker build -t app:a1b2c3d -t app:1.4.2 -t app:staging .
docker push app:a1b2c3d
docker push app:1.4.2
docker push app:staging
```

An immutable identifier -- the git commit SHA (a1b2c3d) or a monotonically increasing CI build number -- is unique per build by construction, and by convention is never reused or repointed, giving you a permanent, precise link from any running container straight back to the exact commit that produced it. A semantic version (1.4.2) is applied deliberately, typically only on release builds, following semver conventions so downstream consumers can reason about compatibility -- and, critically, should be treated as append-only in practice, never re-pushed once published, even though nothing in the tooling itself enforces that by default. A floating convenience tag (staging, edge, nightly) is explicitly expected to move, and that's fine -- it exists for humans browsing a registry UI or spinning up an ad hoc environment, not for anything a production deploy manifest should ever reference directly. The core discipline is which of these three categories a deploy pipeline actually points at: production configuration should reference the immutable identifier or the semver tag (ideally alongside a digest, covered next), never the floating one.

sections.heading: Digest Pinning: The Strongest Guarantee
sections.body:
image@sha256:<digest> pins the literal, content-addressed image itself, immune even to someone repointing a tag -- accidentally, or through a compromised credential pushing a malicious image under an existing, trusted-looking tag name -- to different content later. Referencing app@sha256:9f8e7d... in a deploy manifest guarantees you get exactly that content, no matter what any tag currently happens to point at, which is a categorically stronger guarantee than even a disciplined, never-reused semver tag, since a tag is still, mechanically, just a reassignable pointer someone with sufficient access could repoint regardless of your own team's conventions around it.

The trade-off is readability and tooling overhead: a raw sha256 digest means nothing to a human glancing at a deploy log or a config file the way app:1.4.2 does, so serious setups typically keep both together -- a human-readable tag for reference, and the actual digest as the thing that's genuinely pinned and enforced, for example in a commit message or deploy record reading 'deploying app:1.4.2 (sha256:9f8e7d...)'. GitOps-style deployment tooling and CI pipelines that write the resolved digest into a deployment manifest automatically, right after a successful build and push, are the common way to get this rigor without requiring a human to manually copy a 64-character hash by hand on every release.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes That Undermine Even a Good Tagging Scheme
sections.body:
A subtle failure mode is fixing tagging discipline for your own application's image while leaving FROM some-base:latest (or an unpinned version) in the Dockerfile that builds it -- the exact same mutable-pointer problem, just one level earlier in the pipeline, and one this curriculum's reproducibility module already covered in detail; a rigorously-tagged application image built FROM a floating base image is still not fully reproducible, because the base layer underneath it can silently change between builds.

Another common mistake is having CI push every single build as :latest 'as a matter of habit,' in addition to whatever other tags it applies, without also always emitting an immutable identifier tag for every build, not only release builds -- if the immutable tag only gets applied on 'real' releases, every intermediate build (a hotfix, a debugging build, an experiment someone deployed briefly to a shared environment) loses traceability the moment nobody happens to remember exactly which commit it came from. And a third mistake is assuming a semver-looking tag is automatically as immutable as a git tag -- by default, nothing in a registry stops a careless or rushed team member from re-pushing over an already-published app:1.4.2 with different content, silently invalidating any digest or provenance record anyone previously captured for it; registries that support an explicit 'immutable tags' setting (offered by ECR, GHCR, and others) can enforce this as a genuine, registry-side guarantee rather than a convention people have to remember to honor by hand.

examples.title: Tagging One Build Three Ways
examples.code:
$ GIT_SHA=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
$ docker build -t app:$GIT_SHA -t app:1.4.2 -t app:staging .
$ docker push app:$GIT_SHA      # immutable, traceable back to this exact commit
$ docker push app:1.4.2         # semver, treated as append-only by team convention
$ docker push app:staging       # floating -- expected to move on every future build
examples.explanation: All three tags point at the exact same underlying image content immediately after this sequence runs -- the difference between them is purely about what each is used for and what guarantee it's expected to hold going forward. app:$GIT_SHA will never be reused for a different build, since a new commit produces a new SHA by construction, making it the most reliable way to answer 'what code produced this running container' months later. app:1.4.2 carries the same guarantee only by team discipline -- nothing technical stops a future push from reusing it, which is exactly why registries offering an explicit tag-immutability setting are worth turning on for version tags specifically. app:staging is deliberately expected to be overwritten by the next build that gets promoted to staging, and referencing it anywhere in a production deploy config would be a mistake -- it's meant for humans and ad hoc environments, not for anything requiring a stable target.

examples.title: :latest Repointed Mid-Rollout, Causing Replica Drift
examples.code:
# t=0: deploy tool starts a rolling restart of 4 replicas, all pulling app:latest
$ kubectl rollout restart deployment/app   # (illustrative -- same issue applies to any orchestrator)

# t=0: replica 1 pulls -- gets version A (whatever :latest currently points at)
# t=5s: replica 2 pulls -- gets version A

# t=8s: a DIFFERENT pipeline finishes and pushes a new build to app:latest -- now points at version B

# t=10s: replica 3 pulls -- gets version B
# t=15s: replica 4 pulls -- gets version B
# Result: 2 replicas running version A, 2 running version B, simultaneously, from ONE rollout
examples.explanation: Nothing about this rollout itself is misconfigured -- each replica correctly pulled 'whatever app:latest currently points at' at the moment it happened to pull. The problem is that :latest's mapping changed in the middle of the rollout window, because of an entirely separate pipeline run that had no coordination with this rollout at all. The result is two different versions of the application serving traffic side by side, with no error, warning, or indication in any single replica's own logs that anything unusual happened -- discovering this requires actively comparing what each replica is actually running, which is precisely the kind of debugging burden a tagging scheme built on immutable identifiers avoids by construction, since an immutable tag or digest can never be repointed out from under an in-progress rollout.

examples.title: Pinning a Deploy to a Digest
examples.code:
# docker-compose.yml or a Kubernetes manifest, referencing a digest rather than a tag
services:
  api:
    image: myregistry.example.com/team/app@sha256:9f8e7d6c5b4a3928374658493827465849382746584938274658493827465

# Deploy record / commit message convention pairing the human-readable tag with the pinned digest:
# "Deploying app:1.4.2 (sha256:9f8e7d...) to production"
examples.explanation: Referencing the image by @sha256:<digest> rather than by :1.4.2 or any other tag means this deploy configuration is completely immune to any future repointing of any tag -- even if someone, through error or a compromised credential, later pushes different content under the app:1.4.2 tag, this specific deployment config still resolves to the exact original content, because a digest reference bypasses tag resolution entirely and names the manifest directly. Keeping the human-readable tag alongside the digest in deploy records or commit messages preserves the convenience of 'oh, that's the 1.4.2 release' for a human reading history later, while the digest itself is what's actually being enforced at deploy time.

misconceptions.description: :latest always refers to the most recently built or most stable image in a repository -- that's what the name means.
misconceptions.clarification: :latest is simply the tag Docker applies by default to any build or push that doesn't specify a tag explicitly -- it carries no enforced meaning of recency or stability whatsoever. Whoever has push access can point it at anything: an experimental branch build, a broken hotfix, or a stable release, and the tag itself provides no way to distinguish between those cases after the fact. Treating the name as a promise about what it contains is reading meaning into a string that the tooling itself never guaranteed.

misconceptions.description: Once an image is tagged with a version number, like v1.4.2, that tag is permanently locked to that exact content, the same way a git tag is.
misconceptions.clarification: By default, a registry places no restriction on re-pushing to an existing tag, version-looking or not -- app:1.4.2 can be silently overwritten with entirely different content by a later push unless the registry has an explicit tag-immutability feature turned on (offered by services like ECR and GHCR) or the team simply never does it by disciplined convention. Unlike a git tag, which is cryptographically tied to a specific commit and considered a serious violation to move, a registry tag is a plain, mutable pointer with no such enforcement unless you specifically configure one.

exercises.prompt: Four replicas of a service pull app:latest during a rolling restart, one at a time, a few seconds apart. Partway through, an unrelated CI pipeline finishes a build and pushes a new image to app:latest. What is the likely end state across the four replicas, and why?
exercises.code:
# replica 1 pulls at t=0s
# replica 2 pulls at t=5s
# [unrelated pipeline pushes a NEW build to app:latest at t=8s]
# replica 3 pulls at t=10s
# replica 4 pulls at t=15s
hints: Each replica independently resolves app:latest to whatever digest that tag currently points at, at the exact moment it pulls -- not at the moment the rollout started.
The push at t=8s changes what app:latest points to for every pull AFTER that moment, but has no effect on pulls that already completed before it.
Compare which replicas pulled before versus after t=8s.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Replicas 1 and 2 (pulled at t=0s and t=5s, before the new push) end up running the OLD image content; replicas 3 and 4 (pulled at t=10s and t=15s, after the new push) end up running the NEW image content. The rollout ends with two different versions of the application running simultaneously, purely due to pull timing relative to the unrelated push.
exercises.solutionExplanation: :latest is resolved independently by each replica at the moment it actually performs its pull -- there is no snapshotting of 'what latest meant when this rollout started' shared across the replicas. Replicas 1 and 2 pulled before the unrelated pipeline's push at t=8s, so they received whatever content latest pointed to at that earlier moment; replicas 3 and 4 pulled after that push, receiving the new content instead. The rollout completes with a split population -- two replicas on one version, two on another -- with nothing in any individual replica's logs indicating this happened, since each one correctly did exactly what it was told: pull whatever latest currently resolves to, at whatever moment it happened to ask.

exercises.prompt: A production deploy of app:latest introduces a severe bug. The on-call engineer tries to roll back by redeploying app:latest again, assuming that will restore the previous working version, but it just redeploys the exact same broken build. Explain what went wrong and propose the tagging change that would have made a real rollback possible.
exercises.code:
$ docker pull app:latest && docker run -d app:latest   # "rollback" attempt -- pulls the SAME broken build again
# still broken -- because :latest was never repointed away from the broken build in the first place
hints: Redeploying the same tag a second time resolves to the same content it already resolved to -- what would actually need to change for a redeploy to produce something different?
Was there ever a separate, still-existing reference to 'the previous working build' anywhere the engineer could target directly?
The fix is establishing an immutable tag (or digest) per build BEFORE this incident, not something that can be added retroactively during it.
exercises.solutionCode:
# What the pipeline SHOULD have been doing all along, before this incident:
$ docker build -t app:$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) -t app:latest .
$ docker push app:$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
$ docker push app:latest

# Then a real rollback becomes possible, by targeting the PREVIOUS known-good immutable tag directly:
$ docker pull app:9f8e7d6   # the commit SHA of the last known-good build
$ docker run -d app:9f8e7d6
exercises.solutionExplanation: The rollback attempt failed because it redeployed the same tag, app:latest, which still resolves to the same broken content it already pointed at -- 'redeploy latest again' doesn't move the pointer backward to anything; there's no history built into a tag to roll back through. The actual bug is upstream of the incident: because the pipeline only ever pushed app:latest, with no separate immutable tag per build, there was no other reference anywhere that still pointed specifically at the last known-good version once latest itself was overwritten by the broken build. Fixing this requires the pipeline to push an immutable identifier tag (the git SHA, here) alongside latest on every single build, not just the broken one -- once that convention exists, a real rollback becomes a matter of deploying app:<previous-good-sha> directly, which resolves reliably to that exact previous content regardless of whatever app:latest currently points at, and requires no rebuild, no guessing, and no hoping a rebuild would even be reproducible.

assessments.prompt: What does the tag :latest actually guarantee about the image it points to?
options: That it is the most recently built image in the repository, chronologically.
That it has passed the team's test suite and is considered production-ready.
Nothing beyond being whatever content was most recently pushed under that specific tag name -- it carries no enforced meaning about recency, stability, or quality.
That it matches the highest semantic version number currently published in the repository.
assessments.explanation: Option 3 is correct: :latest is simply the tag Docker applies by default to an unspecified push, and a registry enforces no relationship between that name and actual recency, test status, or version ordering -- it points at whatever was most recently pushed under that literal tag, by whoever had access, full stop. Option 1 sounds plausible but isn't guaranteed -- a team could push an older or unrelated build under :latest at any time, deliberately or by mistake, and nothing prevents it. Option 2 invents a testing/quality guarantee the tag mechanism has no way to enforce or even represent. Option 4 confuses :latest with a genuinely different, semver-aware convention that some tooling implements on top of tags, but which is not what the literal string 'latest' itself means or checks.

assessments.prompt: During a rolling deploy, four replicas independently pull app:latest at slightly different times. Partway through, an unrelated pipeline pushes a new build to app:latest. What is the likely result?
options: All four replicas end up running whichever version was pulled first, since Docker caches that initial resolution for the whole rollout.

Replicas that pulled before the new push end up running the old version, and replicas that pulled after end up running the new version -- resulting in two different versions running simultaneously, with no error surfaced anywhere.
The rollout fails outright, since Docker detects the tag was repointed mid-rollout and aborts the operation.
Only the very last replica to pull is affected; the first three are guaranteed to match each other regardless of the timing of the mid-rollout push.
assessments.explanation: Option 2 correctly describes replica drift: each replica resolves app:latest independently, at the exact moment it pulls, with no shared snapshot of 'what latest meant when the rollout started' -- so replicas pulling before versus after the mid-rollout push end up on genuinely different versions, silently. Option 1 invents a caching behavior that doesn't exist; there's no rollout-wide resolution lock. Option 3 is wrong -- Docker has no mechanism to detect or abort based on a tag being repointed during an unrelated rollout. Option 4 is wrong -- any replica pulling after the push picks up the new version, not just the very last one; the split depends on each replica's individual pull timing relative to t=8s, not on rollout position specifically.

assessments.prompt: Why does pinning a production deployment to app@sha256:<digest> provide a stronger guarantee than pinning to app:1.4.2, even if the team has a strict policy of never re-pushing over an existing version tag?
options: There is no meaningful difference -- both are equally strong guarantees as long as the team's policy is actually followed.

A tag, even a disciplined version tag, is still mechanically just a reassignable pointer that someone with sufficient registry access could repoint (by mistake or through a compromised credential); a digest reference bypasses tag resolution entirely and names the exact content directly, immune to any future repointing of any tag.
Digests are a feature only supported by private, self-hosted registries, not Docker Hub, so this comparison doesn't meaningfully apply to public images.
Pinning by digest is functionally identical to pinning by tag, but it happens to execute faster at pull time.
assessments.explanation: Option 2 is correct and matches the concept's core argument for digest pinning: convention and policy are enforced by people, while a digest reference is enforced structurally -- it names content directly and cannot be affected by any tag being repointed, deliberately or accidentally, by anyone with push access. Option 1 is wrong -- policy compliance is exactly the kind of guarantee that can silently fail (a rushed change, a compromised credential), which is precisely what digest pinning is immune to regardless. Option 3 is false -- digests are a standard part of the OCI Distribution Specification, supported by Docker Hub and virtually every other registry. Option 4 is false -- the practical difference is about the strength of the reference's guarantee, not about pull speed, which digest and tag references don't meaningfully differ on.

assessments.prompt: A team currently pushes every CI build to app:latest and deploys that tag directly to production. Explain, concretely, at least two specific production incidents this practice makes more likely or harder to recover from, and describe the tagging scheme you'd propose instead, including how it changes each of those specific incidents.
assessments.modelAnswer: Two concrete failure modes follow directly from deploying a mutable pointer. The first is an impossible rollback: if the current content behind app:latest turns out to be broken, there is no separate, still-valid reference anywhere pointing at whatever the previous, working content was -- the tag was overwritten, and redeploying app:latest again just redeploys the same broken content a second time, because nothing about a redeploy moves the tag's mapping backward. The second is replica drift during a rolling deploy: because each replica in a multi-instance rollout independently resolves app:latest at the moment it happens to pull, an unrelated push landing mid-rollout can leave some replicas running one version and others running a different one, entirely due to pull timing, with no error surfaced anywhere to indicate the running fleet has silently split into two populations. A third, related problem worth mentioning is untraceability during incident response: given a container running from app:latest, there is no way to determine which commit produced it, and by the time anyone investigates, the tag may already point at something else again. The scheme I'd propose has CI push, on every single build, both an immutable identifier tag -- the git commit SHA or a monotonically increasing build number, which is unique per build and never reused -- and, for actual releases, a semantic version tag treated as append-only by convention (and ideally enforced with a registry's tag-immutability setting). Production deploy configuration would reference the immutable tag or, better, the resolved digest directly, never latest. This directly fixes both incidents described above: a rollback becomes 'redeploy the previous known-good immutable tag,' a real, coherent, always-available operation, rather than a no-op; and replica drift during a rollout becomes structurally impossible, because an immutable tag's mapping can never be repointed out from under an in-progress deploy the way latest's can. A floating tag like staging or edge can still exist for humans browsing the registry or spinning up ad hoc environments -- the discipline is entirely about what production's own deploy configuration is allowed to reference.

concepts.title: Container Builds in a CI/CD Pipeline
concepts.description: A mature CI/CD pipeline treats a container image as the one artifact that gets built exactly once per commit and promoted, unchanged, through every environment -- checkout, build, test, scan, tag, and push are ordered stages with real dependencies between them, and getting that order wrong (deploying before tests pass, or rebuilding separately per environment) reopens problems the rest of this subject spent several modules solving.
learningObjectives: Describe the typical stages of a CI/CD pipeline that produces and deploys a container image -- checkout, build, test, scan, tag, push, deploy -- and explain the ordering dependency between them.

Explain the 'build once, promote everywhere' principle: why the same image artifact, not a separately-rebuilt one, should move from staging to production, and where environment-specific differences should actually live instead.

Explain why build caching is harder to get for free on ephemeral CI runners than on a developer's laptop, and describe a concrete mechanism (registry-based cache via --cache-from/--cache-to) that restores it.
Explain where an automated vulnerability scan fits in the pipeline, and what trade-off 'fail the build on any finding' actually makes.
Given a pipeline definition, identify what breaks if a stage is skipped or reordered -- specifically deploying before tests pass, or pushing before scanning.

sections.heading: The Shape of a Typical Pipeline
sections.body:
A pipeline that builds and ships a container image typically runs through a fairly consistent sequence of stages, each depending on the one before it succeeding: checkout pulls the exact commit being built; build runs docker build (very often a multi-stage Dockerfile, from the earlier module, so the pipeline itself doesn't need a separate build environment beyond Docker) to produce the image; test runs the application's automated test suite, ideally against the actual built image or an intermediate test-target stage rather than a separately-assembled environment, so what's tested is as close as possible to what will actually ship; scan runs an automated vulnerability scan against the built image's contents; tag applies the tagging scheme covered in the previous concept -- an immutable identifier at minimum, a semantic version on release builds; push uploads the tagged image to a registry; and deploy, often a separate pipeline or tool entirely (a GitOps controller reconciling a manifest, an orchestrator API call, a rolling update trigger), pulls that specific tag or digest into an environment.

The ordering isn't arbitrary -- each stage's usefulness depends on what happened before it. Testing before pushing means a broken build is caught before it's ever made available to anything that might pull it. Scanning before, or as a gate on, push means a genuinely vulnerable image doesn't become available to whatever downstream systems trust that registry. Tagging with an immutable identifier before push means every image reaching the registry is traceable back to its exact source from the moment it exists there at all, never as an afterthought applied later.

sections.heading: Build Once, Promote the Same Artifact
sections.body:
The central discipline mature pipelines follow is building exactly one image per commit (or release candidate) and moving that literal artifact through staging, and later production, rather than rebuilding separately for each environment. Rebuilding per environment -- even from identical source, even with an unchanged Dockerfile -- reopens precisely the reproducibility problem the earlier 'works on my machine' module addressed: a rebuild that happens at a different time than the first one can silently pull a different resolved version of an unpinned dependency, or a moved floating base image tag, producing an image that's subtly different from what was actually tested in staging, even though nobody intended any difference at all.

Environment-specific differences -- a different database connection string, different feature-flag values, different API credentials -- belong in runtime configuration: environment variables, mounted config files, or a secrets manager, injected when the container actually starts in a given environment, never baked into a separate, environment-specific image variant. The same literal image, referenced by the same immutable tag or digest, runs in staging and then in production; only what's handed to it at startup differs. This is also precisely why 'it passed in staging' is a meaningful, trustworthy statement under this discipline -- it's a claim about the exact artifact that will also run in production, not about some similar-but-separately-built cousin of it.

sections.heading: Caching on Ephemeral Runners
sections.body:
A developer's laptop naturally accumulates a warm Docker build cache across many local builds over time, which is exactly what makes the layer-ordering discipline from the Dockerfile module pay off day to day. A CI runner, by contrast, is very often ephemeral by design -- spun up fresh for a job and destroyed afterward specifically for isolation and reproducibility reasons -- which means it typically starts with zero prior build cache, defeating those same layer-caching benefits by default unless the pipeline explicitly does something to restore them.

Two common mechanisms address this directly. Passing --cache-from with a reference to a previously-pushed image tells BuildKit to attempt to reuse matching layers from that image even though this specific runner has never built anything before, effectively borrowing a warm cache from whatever the last successful build produced. A registry-backed remote cache goes further, storing cache data in the registry itself, separately from any tagged, deployable image, via docker buildx build --cache-to=type=registry,ref=myregistry/app:buildcache --cache-from=type=registry,ref=myregistry/app:buildcache -- any runner, anywhere, working on any branch, can pull from that shared cache location, which matters especially for parallel CI jobs that would otherwise each independently pay the full, uncached cost of every build step.

sections.heading: Scanning as a Pipeline Gate
sections.body:
An automated vulnerability scan (tools like Trivy, Grype, or Docker Scout are common choices) inspects a built image's installed OS packages and language-level dependencies against known-CVE databases, and typically runs right after build, gating whether the image is allowed to proceed to push and deploy at all. The point of placing it there, specifically before push, is that a vulnerable image should ideally never even become available in a registry other systems or teams might trust and pull from -- catching it after it's already been deployed is strictly worse than catching it before it ever left the pipeline.

The real trade-off in configuring a scan to unconditionally fail the build on any HIGH or CRITICAL finding is velocity against false-positive noise: a scanner flags a CVE in any package that's physically present in the image, regardless of whether the running application ever actually exercises the vulnerable code path at all, which means a hard, unconditional fail-on-any-finding policy can block a pipeline over a library that's technically present but functionally irrelevant to the specific vulnerability. Mature setups typically combine a severity threshold (fail only on HIGH/CRITICAL, not every low-severity finding) with an explicit, reviewed, time-bound exception/allowlist process for specific CVEs a team has genuinely assessed as not exploitable in their context -- rather than either extreme of blocking every release over any finding, or disabling scanning's gating power entirely because it occasionally produces noise.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes and Edge Cases
sections.body:
Pushing to the registry before tests or scans have actually passed makes a broken or vulnerable image pullable by anything watching that repository or tag -- including, in some setups, an automated deploy trigger that reacts to any new push landing, regardless of whether it was ever intended to reach that stage yet. The ordering in the pipeline definition needs to genuinely reflect real dependencies, not just a convenient sequence that happens to usually work.

A second, subtler mistake is deploying a locally-built developer image with reasoning like 'it passed on my machine, let me just push it directly' -- this reintroduces the entire class of environment-drift problems CI exists specifically to eliminate, since a developer's local build environment, base image cache state, and even Docker version are not guaranteed identical to CI's, undermining the 'build once' guarantee before it even starts. A third is failing to scope the build cache per branch or pull request: an unscoped shared cache can leak a layer built for one branch into a completely different branch's build, producing results that are hard to reproduce locally and easy to misattribute to an unrelated bug, when the actual cause is a cache-scoping gap in the pipeline configuration itself.

examples.title: A Representative Pipeline, Stage by Stage
examples.explanation: Each stage genuinely depends on the previous one succeeding: test runs against the exact image just built, not a separately-assembled environment; scan runs before tag/push, using --exit-code 1 to make Trivy itself fail the pipeline on any HIGH or CRITICAL finding rather than just reporting one; push only happens after both test and scan have passed; and both deploy stages reference the identical resolved digest, satisfying build-once-promote-everywhere -- production runs the literal same artifact staging already validated, differing only in whatever environment-specific configuration deploy-tool injects for the production environment specifically.

examples.title: Registry-Backed Build Cache on an Ephemeral Runner
examples.explanation: --cache-from tells this build to look for reusable cached layers at the given registry reference, even though this specific CI runner may have never built this project before -- if a previous build already pushed cache data to that same reference, matching layers (base image setup, dependency installation, anything unchanged since that cache was written) are reused instead of re-executed from scratch. --cache-to writes this build's own layer cache back to that same registry reference (mode=max captures cache for intermediate layers too, not just the final stage, which matters for multi-stage Dockerfiles), so the NEXT build -- on this runner, a different runner, or a different branch's pipeline entirely -- can benefit from it in turn. This is what makes Dockerfile layer-caching discipline actually pay off in CI specifically, where a fresh, stateless runner would otherwise start from zero cache on every single run.

examples.title: Build Once, Promote: Same Digest, Different Runtime Config
examples.code:
# Staging deploy
$ docker run -d --name api \
    -e DATABASE_URL=postgres://staging-db:5432/app \
    -e FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT=true \
    myregistry.example.com/app@sha256:9f8e7d6c5b4a...

# Production deploy -- THE SAME IMAGE DIGEST, only the environment variables differ
$ docker run -d --name api \
    -e DATABASE_URL=postgres://prod-db:5432/app \
    -e FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT=false \
    myregistry.example.com/app@sha256:9f8e7d6c5b4a...
examples.explanation: Both deployments reference the exact same image digest -- no rebuild happens between staging and production at all. Every difference between the two environments -- which database to talk to, whether a feature flag is on -- is supplied entirely through environment variables handed to the container at docker run time, never through a separately-built image. This is precisely what makes 'it passed in staging' a meaningful signal about what will happen in production: the literal bytes of the application and its dependencies are identical in both places, and only externally-injected configuration differs, which is exactly the surface area you'd want to differ between environments, and nothing more.

misconceptions.description: Each environment (development, staging, production) should have its own Dockerfile or its own separate rebuild, tuned specifically for that environment.
misconceptions.clarification: This violates the build-once-promote-everywhere principle and reopens the exact reproducibility problems containers are meant to solve: a rebuild at a different time, even from identical source, can silently pull different transitive dependency versions or a moved floating base image tag, producing an image that subtly differs from whatever was actually validated in an earlier environment. Environment-specific differences -- connection strings, feature flags, credentials -- belong in runtime configuration injected at container start (environment variables, mounted config, a secrets manager), not in separately-built, per-environment image variants.

misconceptions.description: Because CI runners are ephemeral and start clean every time, Docker's layer caching from the Dockerfile module simply doesn't apply in a CI pipeline, and there's nothing to be done about that.
misconceptions.clarification: A clean runner does mean there's no local cache sitting around from a previous run by default, but explicit mechanisms restore effective caching anyway: passing --cache-from a previously-pushed image lets a build reuse matching layers even on a runner that's never built this project before, and a registry-backed remote cache (--cache-to/--cache-from with type=registry) stores cache data centrally so any runner, on any branch, can warm its cache from it. Layer-ordering discipline still pays off in CI -- it just requires an explicit cache-sourcing mechanism that a developer's laptop gets for free simply by not being destroyed between builds.

exercises.prompt: A pipeline is defined with these stages in this order: build, push, test, scan, deploy. A commit introduces a bug that the test suite would catch. Predict what happens, and identify exactly which stage ordering problem allowed it.
hints: push happens before test in this ordering -- what does that mean about whether a broken image is ever made available before it's actually validated?
If anything else (another pipeline, an automated deploy trigger, a teammate) is watching this repository/tag for new pushes, what could it do before this pipeline even reaches its own test stage?
The pytest failure will still stop THIS pipeline's own deploy stage -- the problem is what already happened in the meantime, not that deploy itself proceeds.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The broken image is pushed to the registry BEFORE the test stage even runs, meaning it becomes pullable by anything watching that tag -- another system, an automated deploy trigger, a teammate -- during the window between push and the eventual test failure. Once pytest fails, THIS pipeline's own deploy stage correctly never runs, but the image had already been made available externally in the meantime, which push-before-test was never supposed to allow.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Because push comes before test in this pipeline's ordering, the broken image is uploaded to the registry and becomes pullable by anything with access to it -- immediately, regardless of what the later test stage eventually finds. When test does run and pytest fails, this specific pipeline correctly halts before reaching deploy, so THIS pipeline never deploys the broken image itself. But the damage the ordering enables is separate from that: any other system polling the registry for new pushes, an automated staging auto-deploy watching for new tags, or simply a teammate pulling the tag manually during that window could pick up the broken image before the test failure is even known. The fix is reordering so test (and scan) run and must pass BEFORE push, ensuring a broken build is caught and contained entirely within the pipeline, before it's ever made externally available at all.

exercises.prompt: A team maintains three separate Dockerfiles -- Dockerfile.dev, Dockerfile.staging, Dockerfile.prod -- each with slightly different RUN steps, arguing this lets each environment be 'tuned' appropriately. After a recent incident, the team discovers a bug that was never caught in staging because Dockerfile.staging and Dockerfile.prod had quietly drifted -- an environment variable default baked into one but not the other. Diagnose the structural problem and propose the fix.
exercises.code:
# Dockerfile.staging
FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim
...
ENV FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT=true
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

# Dockerfile.prod
FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim
...
# (no ENV FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT line here -- someone forgot to add it when this file was created)
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
hints: Two separately-maintained Dockerfiles for 'the same' application are two separate artifacts that can drift from each other silently, with no tooling forcing them to stay in sync.

The specific drifted setting here -- a feature flag default -- is exactly the kind of thing that belongs in runtime configuration, not baked into an image at build time via ENV in a per-environment Dockerfile.
The structural fix isn't 'remember to keep the Dockerfiles in sync' -- it's having only ONE Dockerfile and ONE built image, with environment differences supplied at deploy time instead.
exercises.solutionCode:
# ONE Dockerfile, no environment-specific ENV defaults for things that should vary by environment:
# Dockerfile
FROM node:20.11.1-bookworm-slim
...
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

# Build ONCE:
$ docker build -t app:${GIT_SHA} .
$ docker push app:${GIT_SHA}

# Supply the environment-specific value at deploy time, per environment, instead of at build time:
$ docker run -d -e FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT=true  app@sha256:... # staging
$ docker run -d -e FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT=false app@sha256:... # production (same digest)
exercises.solutionExplanation: The root cause is having three separately-maintained Dockerfiles at all -- each one is an independent artifact that can drift from the others with zero tooling enforcing consistency between them, and this incident is exactly that: a feature-flag default that existed in one file and was simply never added to another, an easy, invisible mistake with no build-time error to catch it, since each Dockerfile builds successfully on its own. Baking an environment-specific value into an image via ENV in a per-environment Dockerfile is also the wrong layer for that value to live at in the first place -- feature flags, connection strings, and similar configuration are exactly what belongs in runtime configuration, supplied when a container starts, not compiled into the image itself. The structural fix collapses this to one Dockerfile, building one image per commit, with FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT and anything else environment-specific supplied via -e (or an orchestrator's equivalent) at deploy time, per environment -- staging and production then run the literal same image digest, and any future flag or config difference is visible directly in each environment's own deploy configuration, rather than hidden as a silent discrepancy between two independently hand-maintained Dockerfiles.

assessments.prompt: Under the 'build once, promote everywhere' principle, how should a difference in database connection string between staging and production typically be handled?
options: By maintaining two separate Dockerfiles, one per environment, each with the correct connection string baked in via ENV.
By rebuilding the image separately for staging and for production, each build using the appropriate connection string as a build argument.
By building the image once and supplying the connection string as runtime configuration (an environment variable or mounted config) when the container starts in each environment.
By hardcoding both connection strings into the application code and having it detect which environment it's running in at startup.
assessments.explanation: Option 3 is correct and is exactly the build-once-promote-everywhere principle in practice: one image, built once, is promoted unchanged through every environment, with purely environmental differences like a connection string supplied externally at container-start time. Option 1 and option 2 both involve producing more than one actual image artifact for what should be a single promoted artifact, reopening reproducibility risk and configuration drift between environments, which is precisely the failure mode this principle exists to prevent. Option 4 hardcodes environment-specific values into the application's own source, which is more rigid and harder to change than externalized runtime configuration, and still doesn't address the core problem of what artifact should move between environments.

assessments.prompt: Why doesn't Docker's layer-caching discipline from the Dockerfile module automatically pay off on a typical CI runner the way it does on a developer's laptop?
options: CI runners use a fundamentally different filesystem type that is structurally incompatible with layer caching.

CI runners are frequently ephemeral, spun up fresh for a job and destroyed afterward, so they typically start with zero prior build cache unless the pipeline explicitly restores it via a mechanism like --cache-from pointing at a previously-pushed image, or a registry-backed remote cache.
Docker deliberately disables build caching inside any CI environment, as a hard-coded security restriction.
Layer caching only works for single-stage Dockerfiles, and CI pipelines exclusively build using multi-stage Dockerfiles.
assessments.explanation: Option 2 correctly identifies the actual cause: a fresh, ephemeral runner has no accumulated local cache the way a long-lived laptop does, so the same layer-ordering discipline that pays off for free locally requires an explicit cache-restoration mechanism -- --cache-from/--cache-to against a registry -- to have any effect in CI. Option 1 is false -- there's no filesystem-level incompatibility; the issue is purely about what cache state happens to already exist on a given machine. Option 3 is false -- Docker imposes no such CI-specific restriction; caching works identically, it just has nothing to reuse on a clean runner by default. Option 4 is false -- layer caching applies to both single- and multi-stage Dockerfiles equally, and CI pipelines use both kinds.

assessments.prompt: A pipeline is ordered build -> push -> test -> scan -> deploy. A commit introduces a bug the test suite would catch. What specifically goes wrong because of this ordering, even though the pipeline's own deploy stage never runs the broken image?
options: Nothing goes wrong, since the pipeline itself never actually deploys the broken image to production.

The broken image is uploaded to the registry and becomes pullable by anything watching that repository or tag -- another automated deploy trigger, a different pipeline, or a teammate -- during the window between push and the eventual test failure, even though this pipeline's own deploy stage correctly never runs.
The push stage itself automatically fails if the image being pushed contains a bug, regardless of test results.
Docker registries automatically quarantine any image that later fails a test run after having already been pushed.
assessments.explanation: Option 2 correctly identifies the real risk of this ordering: pushing before testing makes the broken image externally available -- to other systems, pipelines, or people watching that tag -- during exactly the window before the test failure is even known, regardless of whether this specific pipeline's own deploy stage ever runs. Option 1 understates the risk by only considering this pipeline's own deploy stage, ignoring everything else that might already be watching the registry. Option 3 is false -- push has no awareness of application-level bugs; it's a pure data-transfer operation. Option 4 is false -- registries have no such automatic quarantine mechanism tied to a separate pipeline's later test results.

assessments.prompt: Explain why placing an automated vulnerability scan immediately after the build stage, and gating push on it passing, is considered good pipeline design -- and explain the real cost/trade-off of configuring that gate to fail the build on any finding at all, no matter how minor.
assessments.modelAnswer: Placing the scan right after build and gating push on its result means a vulnerable image never becomes available in a registry that other systems, teams, or automated deploy triggers might trust and pull from -- catching a known vulnerability before the image ever leaves the pipeline is strictly better than catching it after it's already been deployed somewhere, at which point remediation requires an active response rather than simply not shipping the problem in the first place. It also keeps the registry itself trustworthy as a source: anything that successfully pulls an image from that repository can have some baseline confidence it already passed this check, rather than needing to independently re-verify every image it consumes. The trade-off in making the gate fail on any finding whatsoever, regardless of severity, is a real cost in pipeline velocity versus the actual security benefit gained. A vulnerability scanner flags a CVE based purely on the presence of a matching package version in the image -- it generally has no visibility into whether the running application actually exercises the specific vulnerable code path in that package at all. This means an unconditional fail-on-any-finding policy will routinely block releases over vulnerabilities that are technically present in the image but functionally irrelevant to what the application does, which trains teams to either ignore scan failures as noise (defeating the entire point of the gate) or to spend disproportionate time chasing down and patching things that pose negligible real risk, at the cost of shipping actual fixes and features more slowly. The common, more mature middle ground is a severity threshold -- failing specifically on HIGH and CRITICAL findings rather than every finding -- paired with an explicit, reviewed, time-bound exception process for specific CVEs a team has assessed and determined aren't exploitable in their particular context, so the gate stays meaningful and trusted rather than becoming something people route around.
